Description: The principal component (PC)-based indices of the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) are the time series of the leading Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) of SLP anomalies over the Atlantic sector, 20°-80°N, 90°W-40°E. These indices are used to measure the NAO throughout the year, tracking the seasonal movements of the Icelandic low and Azores high. These movements are illustrated in the Figures on this page. Positive values of the NAO index are typically associated with stronger-than-average westerlies over the middle latitudes, more intense weather systems over the North Atlantic and wetter/milder weather over western Europe.
Motivation:
Indicandum: Large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns over the North Atlantic region, and more specifically the strengths of the jet-stream/westerlies.
Motivation: The westerlies and the jet-stream is of fundamental importance to weather and the marine climate in the Northeast Atlantic, including the Nordic Seas. This involves the strength and the path of winter storms.
ConceptualUnderstanding:
The NAO index is a fundamental metric of weather patterns, ocean circulation, and marine ecosystem variability across the North Atlantic and Norwegian Sea. It reflects wind patterns, heat transport, precipitation, sea surface temperatures, and consequently affects primary productivity, species distributions, and fisheries. Essential for ecosystem status summary as it provides context for understanding climate-driven ecosystem changes and supports predictive capabilities in IEA frameworks. The indicator-indicandum relationship is generally stable but can exhibit non-stationarity on multidecadal timescales (e.g. when the explanatory power of NAO decreased in the mid-1990s).
Positive NAO phases indicate stronger-than-normal pressure gradients, leading to stronger westerlies, milder winters in northern Europe, increased storminess, and enhanced northward heat transport. Negative phases produce opposite effects with weaker westerlies and colder northern European conditions.
ScientificConsensus:
There is strong scientific foundation spanning over a century of research. The relationship between NAO and North Atlantic climate/ocean variability is well-documented through observational and modeling studies.
The NAO is widely recognized as the dominant mode of atmospheric variability in the North Atlantic. It sused extensively across multiple ocean basins and climate systems, is recommended by international institutions and is a standard reference in IPCC assessments and ICES working group reports.
QuantitativeDimension: The NAO index quantifies the normalized pressure difference between the Icelandic Low and Azores High pressure systems, and is thus a quantitative standardized dimensionless index values. The index is derved using the Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF / PCA) approach, which is a method used in reanalysis-based climate studies. Here, gridded sea level pressure anomalies across the North Atlantic sector (usually 20°N–80°N, 90°W–40°E) are used in an Empirical Orthogonal Function or Principal Component Analysis and the first mode (EOF1) typically represents the NAO pattern — a dipole of opposite pressure anomalies between the subtropical and subpolar regions.  The NAO index is derived back to 1950 by this method.
Precision: It has high precision and is in its essence based on well-calibrated meteorological data with long-term stability. Signal-to-noise ratio is high for monthly and seasonal averages
Bias: Relative changes are highly trustworthy; absolute values are meaningful when using standardized calculation periods.
Updating: Monthly updates available typically within 1-2 weeks of month end. Real-time estimates available with ~5-day delay. Some providers offer daily updates.
SpaceTimeCoverage:
Spatial: Basin-scale index representing North Atlantic atmospheric circulation (approximately 20-70°N, 90°W-40°E). Directly relevant to Norwegian Sea ecosystem scale. 
Temporal: Available from 1899 onwards.
LevelOfIntegration: The index represents the physical environment and atmospheric circulation system. It integrates across multiple spatial scales.
Cost: The cost is low for WGINOR. Data is freely available and requires minimal computational resources and basic statistical expertise. Funding security is excellent as based on operational meteorological networks with long-term governmental commitment.
History: Multiple calculation methodologies exist. Some methodological evolution but generally consistent.
Simplicity: The EOF/PC analysis of se level pressure fields is advanced, but is a accepted and used across research institutions.
Transparency: Calculation method is well-documented and standardized. Multiple data providers offer complete methodological documentation. Data and code freely available. Meets FAIR principles fully. Historical versions and metadata well-maintained.
Sensitivity: There is high sensitivity to large-scale atmospheric circulation changes. The response is generally linear to pressure gradient changes but can show non-linear relationships during extreme phases. Variations directly reflect changes in the North Atlantic pressure dipole strength and position.
Specificity: There is high specificity for North Atlantic atmospheric circulation patterns. Changes can be attributed specifically to shifts in the Icelandic Low/Azores High system. However, can be influenced by teleconnections from other climate modes (e.g., ENSO, QBO). Generally unambiguous interpretation for seasonal/annual scales.
LagAndLeadTime: There is immediate response to atmospheric changes (no lag). Limited predictive skill beyond ~2 weeks for specific values, but seasonal forecasting shows some skill. Seasonal forecasts are available from major meteorological centers. The indicandum is found to lead key oceanographic processes (e.g. the meridional position of the Gulf Stream) by 1-2 years.
ManagementRelevance: NAO is reported by ICES in working group reports and climate summaries and is a key indicator in various national climate monitoring programs.
ManagementUse: NAO is primarily used for surveilling climate variability. It is not used in management or decision making.
ReferencePoint: Both NAO phases have different ecosystem implications. Positive NAO is generally associated with increased storm activity over North Atlantic and western Europe, enhanced precipitation and higher temperatures over Northern Europe and reduced precipitation and lower temperatures over Southern Europe. Negative NAO is associated with the opposite as beforementioned.
PriorKnowledge: The indicator is well known among marine scientists and meteorologists, but less known among managers and among the public. It is well-established in scientific literature across disciplines.
Clarity: Moderate to high clarity for scientific audiences. Requires some explanation for non-specialists to understand implications. Index values (e.g., +1.5, -0.8) need contextualization. Uncertainties are minimal and easy to communicate.
Reaction: Public/policy reactions may be limited due to abstract nature of index. Most effective when combined with impact-based communication showing ecosystem consequences.

FullName: Mackerel average weight at age 3 in the stock
Description: Input for annual analytical stock assessment released by ICES in October. Data compile by WGWIDE. Weight-at-age (age 3) in the stock calculated as the average of the weight-at-age in three areas, corresponding to definition of the former spawning components, weighted by the relative mackerel biomass in each area (as estimated by the 2022 egg survey for the southern and western areas and the 2017 egg survey for the North Sea area). Mean weight-at-age in 2022 for the western area are estimated from Dutch, Irish and German commercial catch data, the biological sampling data taken during the egg surveys and during the Norwegian tagging survey. Only samples corresponding to mature fish, from areas and periods corresponding to spawning, as defined at the 2014 benchmark assessment (ICES, 2014) and laid out in the Stock Annex, were used to compute the mean weight-at-age in the western spawning area. For the North Sea area, mean weight-at-age in 2022 were calculated from samples of the commercial catches collected from Divisions 4.a and 4.b in the second quarter of 2022. Stock weights for the southern area, are based on samples from the Spanish catches and surveys in Divisions 8.c and 9a in the 2nd quarter of the year. The mean weights in the three area and in the stock in 2022 are shown in table 8.5.2.
